General News & Research.title: Robo-soldier startup backed by Eric Trump misses payroll, may collapse
General News & Research.author: Jeremy Hsu
General News & Research.excerpt: A humanoid robotics company backed and advised by President Donald Trump’s son, Eric Trump, has reportedly missed payroll and may be on the brink of collapse after a funding shortfall. The Silicon Valley startup, Foundation Future Industries, claims it is developing and testing robots for military roles on battlefields from Ukraine to Gaza. Foundation failed to pay employees for the payroll period ending on October 30, anonymous sources told CNBC . The startup’s staff is especially angry because Foundation’s co-founder and CEO, Sankaet Pathak , supposedly borrowed $4.6 million in company funds to buy a luxury home overlooking San Francisco Bay about a year ago. This comes as Pathak and Foundation’s leadership are still looking to raise funding to support a $3 billion valuation, based on their promise to develop a humanoid robot ready for combat duty and capable of wielding various weapons. Read full article Comments

General News & Research.title: Three small failures combined to take down Microsoft 365
General News & Research.author: Nick Indge
General News & Research.excerpt: A hidden defect in Microsoft's cloud gateway, dormant since July, was to blame for one of the largest outages in the company's history last week. A preliminary Post-Incident Report (PIR) released by the company outlines how the latent bug, changes in traffic, and reduced server capacity combined to knock much of Microsoft 365 and Exchange infrastructure offline at the end of last week. Microsoft's report lists the incident's final status as "a technical issue not related to cyber or AI/agents." Microsoft's preliminary report places the outage between November 12 at 16:20 UTC and November 13 at 16:10 UTC, just under 24 hours total, and additional monitoring remained in place for any affected systems through November 14. The outage started on November 12 and quickly rippled through businesses and public offices that depend on Microsoft's cloud and email exchange infrastructure. The outage is covered in Microsoft's incident IDs EX1550543 and MO1550821. You need Microsoft 365 admin credentials to see the full report on the company's status pages, but Office Watch has reproduced the preliminary report , and the University of Pennsylvania maintains an archive of Microsoft's service-health updates . Read full article Comments

General News & Research.title: Hyperscale data centers use 2% of US electricity
General News & Research.author: Scott K. Johnson
General News & Research.excerpt: One flashpoint for the tech industry’s all-in push on large language models has been the sudden rush to turn investment money into hyperscale data centers. The rush hasn’t allowed anyone to plan how to supply the required electricity cleanly or with minimal impact on ratepayers. Instead, it has been difficult to even collect information on what’s being built. A new study has tallied energy use and estimated emissions for hyperscalers operating in the United States between May 2024 and April 2025. They weren’t able to differentiate between AI compute and more traditional data services, but it provides a clear point of reference to track moving forward. Finding the centers The team started with a list of 675 facilities from a commercial database based on news reports, company statements, and satellite imagery. They dropped any that didn’t have a reported electrical capacity or that they couldn’t verify was a suitably large building with the expected cooling and electrical connection equipment. That reduced the list to 403 data centers with an average electrical capacity of about 40 megawatts. Read full article Comments

General News & Research.title: Shareholders sue Intel, its CEO, and CFO after stock drops 28.6 percent in one day
General News & Research.author: Scharon Harding
General News & Research.excerpt: Intel is being sued by shareholders, who are accusing the chipmaker of misleading them about the impact of the PC sales slump that contributed to a drop of 28.6 percent in the price of Intel's stock on October 30. The lawsuit ( PDF ), filed on Friday in the San Jose, California, federal court, is seeking class-action certification and lists the City of Southfield Fire and Police Retirement System and “all others similarly situated” as plaintiffs. In addition to Intel, Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan and Intel’s EVP and CFO David Zinsner are listed as defendants. The plaintiffs claim that Intel made “materially false and misleading statements and omissions” between July 23 and October 29. They are seeking unspecified compensatory damages, plus legal and other associated fees, for shareholders during that period. Read full article Comments

General News & Research.title: Comcast's "fiber-powered Wi-Fi" is just cable, AT&T says in false advertising case
General News & Research.author: Jon Brodkin
General News & Research.excerpt: AT&T on Friday accused Comcast of false advertising in a lawsuit challenging the marketing claim that Comcast's cable broadband service and Wi-Fi is "fiber-powered." "This case challenges Comcast’s false advertising campaign for its residential Internet service, marketed under the Xfinity brand to consumers nationwide," AT&T's lawsuit said. "At the center of that campaign is Comcast’s claim that Xfinity Internet and its associated Wi-Fi service are 'Fiber-Powered.'" While Comcast has deployed plenty of fiber throughout the US, its cable Internet service makes the final connection to homes with coaxial cable. This results in upload speeds being far slower than download speeds. Read full article Comments

General News & Research.repository_description: AG-UI: the Agent-User Interaction Protocol. Bring Agents into Frontend Applications.
General News & Research.readme_excerpt: ### The open protocol that connects any agent to any app. **[Docs](https://docs.ag-ui.com)** · **[Examples](https://dojo.ag-ui.com)** · **[Spec](https://docs.ag-ui.com/spec/1.0)** · **[Discord](https://discord.gg/Jd3FzfdJa8)** **AG-UI is an open, lightweight, event-based protocol that standardizes how AI agents connect to user-facing applications.** Agents don't fit the request/response model. They stream tokens, call tools mid-response, update shared state, pause for a human, and spawn subagents, and every framework does it differently. AG-UI replaces that custom wiring with one bi-directional event stream: the agent emits typed events, and any client can render them, no matter which framework built the agent. The same agent can power a web app, a mobile app, a terminal, or Slack. > [!IMPORTANT] > **AG-UI 1.0 is here.** The protocol now has a stable, frozen [specification](https://docs.ag-ui.com/spec/1.0) backed by a JSON Schema, and the TypeScript, Python, and .NET SDKs are generated from it. 1.0 is backwards compatible in both directions: 0.x agents work with 1.0 clients and vice versa. [What changed →](https://docs.ag-ui.com/spec/1.0/changelog) · [Migration guide →](https://docs.ag-ui.com/migrating-to-1-0) ## Quick start **Start a new app.** The CLI scaffolds a frontend ([CopilotKit](https://github.com/CopilotKit/CopilotKit) on Next.js, or a terminal client) wired to the agent framework you pick: ```bash npx create-ag-ui-app@latest ``` Then follow the printed next steps.…

It is available as a Model-Context-Protocol (MCP) server and as a [CLI][cli]. General News & Research.readme_excerpt: # Claude Trading Skills **Data handling:** [Privacy policy](docs/en/privacy.md) · [Security policy](SECURITY.md) Claude Trading Skills started as a personal project to use AI to improve my own trading process. Claude Trading Skills is a Claude Skills-based trading workflow toolkit for time-constrained individual investors. It is designed for investors who use long-term investing, ETFs, and dividend stocks as their core, while using disciplined swing trading as a satellite strategy when market conditions are favorable. The goal is not to outsource buy/sell decisions to AI. The goal is to structure market review, risk management, trade planning, journaling, and continuous improvement. It is open source because the workflows, checklists, and review habits behind better trading decisions can improve through shared practice. This is not a signal service or a promise of profitability. It is a toolkit for traders who want to build a better decision process. Key Features • How To Use • Installation • Customization • Project goals, alternatives [English] [ 中文 ] [ 日本語 ] [ 한국어 ] [ Русский ] ### Syntax highlighting `bat` supports syntax highlighting for a large number of programming and markup languages: ![Syntax highlighting example](https://imgur.com/rGsdnDe.png) ### Git integration `bat` communicates with `git` to show modifications with respect to the index (see left sidebar): ![Git integration example](https://i.imgur.com/2lSW4RE.png) ### Show non-printable characters You can use the `-A`/`--show-all` option to show and highlight non-printable characters: ![Non-printable character example](https://i.imgur.com/WndGp9H.png) ### Automatic paging By default, `bat` pipes its own output to a pager (e.g. `less`) if the output is too large for one screen. If you would rather `bat` work like `cat` all the time (never page output), you can set `--paging=never` as an option, either on the command line or in your configuration file. If you intend to alias `cat` to `bat` in your shell configuration, you can use `alias cat='bat --paging=never'` to preserve the default behavior. #### File concatenation Even with a pager set, you can still use `bat` to concatenate files :wink:. Whenever `bat` detects a non-interactive terminal (i.e. when you pipe into another process or into a file), `bat` will act as a drop-in replacement for `cat` and fall back to printing the plain file contents…

General News & Research.title: Show HN: Startup funding simulator
General News & Research.author: zikero
General News & Research.story_text: Hi HN We built a tool to help founders understand how modern fundraising (with safes) works, and how much dilution you can expect when raising money. The project is open-source. The code is a mess right now, but it'll get better I promise. You can also help with that. We didn't build this to make money. We genuinely did it because we were looking for it, and couldn't find it. We're in fact in the process of fundraising for a company, and at first glance the process looks simple. Just an excel sheet will do! But then the more we dug into it and tried different simulators, the more we realized that it's more complex than it looks. We even signed up to Pulley, Carta and others just to run simulations. But they're a bit confusing. TL;DR: Understanding modern startup funding and knowing how much dilution you'll face is hard. We built a tool that'll hopefully help with that. You can add Post-money Safes, priced rounds and issue options to employees, and you can see how that affects your ownership at every step. You can also simulate an Exit scenario and see how much money you'll be left with. --- Some examples of complex stuff: - There are many different types of safes. They all convert at the first priced round, but in different ways. Some are through discount, some are uncapped, some have a fixed valuation cap, and some have both a discount and a valuation cap. - All safes (before first priced round) convert at the same time. They don't dilute each other, which is what happens…

AI / AI Tools / AI Agents.description:
Anthropic just released Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, and while it is easily the most capable public model in the world across long-horizon coding, robotics, hardware design, and theoretical physics, the biggest story is buried in the fine print. For the first time, Anthropic admits it deliberately limited Fable 5.2 during training on accelerator kernel optimization and LLM architecture research so those specific skills stay capped at Opus 5.5 levels. We break down how today's release confirms Fable 5.2 is METR's Model 3, why the unreleased Model 4 and Anthropic's secret NanoGPT-style autonomous experiment scaffold are grazing the recursive self-improvement threshold, and test Fable 5.2 live on a custom game and LLM benchmark.

AI / AI Tools / AI Agents.title: Fable 5.2 is CRACKED but THIS goes BEYOND THE MODEL
AI / AI Tools / AI Agents.description:
Fable 5.2 just dropped and most engineers DON'T need it. Everyone has access to the same frontier intelligence. The model is NOT your edge. The system you build around the model is.

One super agent that does everything is a myth. Sub-agents hit a ceiling. Agent swarms burn more money than they make. The real multi-agent sweet spot? Small agent teams.

🚀 Phase 3 PRE-LAUNCH IS LIVE (What if your agents never stopped?)
https://agenticengineer.com/infinite-agentic-engineering?y=hYIymEMB9x4

🔥 In Tiny Software Factories (TSF) Lesson 3, IndyDevDan breaks down small agent teams: a handful of specialized agents, each owning one kind of work, led by a single orchestrator. Picture two agents on the same model. One is generic, with default tools and a context window stuffed with every problem. The other has focused tools, focused context, and a focused system prompt loaded with your team's rules and expertise. The focused agent wins every time, the same way a focused engineer wins.

⚡ Quick Fable 5.2 mention: it's an incredible leap, but you only need it if you're writing massive 500 line specs, hill climbing in a recursive self-improving loop, or running multi-agent orchestration. That third bucket is where software factories get interesting. The system card shows a five agent team beating both a single agent and a pile of async agents. And the real surprise on Artificial Analysis isn't max mode. It's Fable 5.2 medium and low, still out-scoring 70% of the top models at a fraction of the cost. Use it as an orchestrator with workhorse models below it. But remember, the model is just one fourth of the core four: context, model, prompt, tools.

🏭 Every software factory starts as an empty factory. Why? So you can customize it. This is liquid software, designed to be reshaped to YOUR problem.

🛠️ Key takeaways:

Small Agent Teams: Several specialized, durable agents inside one factory, each with its own core four, list, and lane. Hit tilde to open the team switcher and jump between agents, each with its own chat, page, and settings.

The Lead Agent: Your orchestrator and single interface. You talk to one agent, the team does the work. Its only job is managing the team on your behalf, which keeps your cognitive overhead low as you scale.

Human Near The Loop: Through team asks, your agents queue up decisions for your approval, feedback, or rejection. You answer, they unblock. This is the mechanism that moves you from in the loop to near the loop.

💡 The core lesson: your engineering work isn't generic. Specific problems require specialized solutions. When anyone can build anything with one prompt, raw model capability stops being the edge. Proactive AI agents organized into small agent teams, with a lead agent coordinating and you near the loop, are how you outperform a single generic agent.

🌟 This lesson stacks every feature from lessons one and two and takes the empty factory right to the moment it's ready to become a running factory. If you're serious about agentic engineering and want specialized agents solving your specific problems around the clock, this is your playbook. Join Phase 3 of Infinite Agentic Engineering to get your own tiny software factory.

Stay focused and keep building.

AI / AI Tools / AI Agents.title: ZERO to RUNNING Software Factory In 16 Minutes (LIQUID Software)
AI / AI Tools / AI Agents.description:
Stop waiting for the next model. It will not save you. Neither will the next tool or harness. YOU are the bottleneck. 🔥

Every minute you spend prompting back and forth is a minute your agents sit idle waiting on you. The engineers pulling ahead right now are not chasing primitives. They are moving from in the loop to near the loop, where proactive AI agents work around the clock and only stop at decisions that actually need you.

😲 Get Your Tiny Software Factory
https://agenticengineer.com/infinite-agentic-engineering?y=GRlcm3wmOqs

🚀 In this video, we take an empty template and turn it into a running software factory inside a real product codebase, live. One skill, one command, three steps: initialize, configure, specialize. We mount a Tiny Software Factory into Hues, a mock prompt-to-image app, then hand our in-loop agent a 150-line plan that configures it into an AI analytics agent that keeps working after you stop watching.

🏭 IndyDevDan here with Tiny Software Factories lesson two, part of Infinite Agentic Engineering. Lesson one built the foundation. Here we stack 14 new features on top of the empty factory: generic agentic tooling that has no purpose until you give it one. Great defaults plus full customization is a massive advantage, and you can redeploy it against any problem you face on repeat.

💧 The big idea: liquid software. With rising intelligence and falling token costs, a new class of software is emerging that takes the shape of the problem you're solving, and keeps changing shape as you learn more. The Tiny Software Factory is liquid software, designed from day one to be customized by you and by the agent living inside it.

🛠️ Key takeaways:

In Loop vs Near the Loop: In the loop, you are the bottleneck. Near the loop, proactive agents run 24/7 and surface results only when a decision needs you.

Init, Configure, Specialize: Mount the empty factory into any greenfield or brownfield codebase, then pass a detailed plan to the configure skill. Agents building agents.

Tool Summaries: A lightweight model summarizes your agent's tool calls into sentences you can read at a glance. You can look away and pray, or you can engineer and measure.

Specialized Subagents: One-off agents with their own model tier, system prompt, and tools, plus hard time and spend budgets. Every run is traced: prompt in, synthesis, output.

Agentic Access Parity: Every button click and settings change, your agent can do too. One prompt retunes subagent defaults, enables cron pulse, builds a new theme, and rewires the nav bar.

Specialization Wins: One super agent that does everything is not how you solve specialized problems on repeat. Specialization is your advantage. Moving near the loop multiplies it.

💡 Whether you run Claude Code, the Pi coding agent, or your own custom harness, the leverage is the same. Stop fixating on the next model and make the meta optimization in how you work. The scale of intelligence operating on your behalf directly drives the impact you can have with agentic engineering.

🌟 After every lesson, ask yourself: what problems can I repeatedly solve with a tiny software factory? Then build the system that builds the system, and get your butt out of the seat.

AI / AI Tools / AI Agents.title: Tiny Software Factories: Agentic Engineering DONE WRONG
AI / AI Tools / AI Agents.description:
What's up Engineers, here's a SNEAK PEEK of the upcoming Phase 3 Agentic Engineering Course: Tiny Software Factories

Phase 3 PRESALE IS LIVE (What if your agents never stopped?)
https://agenticengineer.com/infinite-agentic-engineering?y=1v7ldJiyH-Y

Today you'll learn agentic engineering DONE WRONG. On purpose. 🤨

You know this... You and I are the bottleneck. Every time you sit in the terminal prompting one agent back and forth, YOU are the system. Eighty percent or more of the work we're doing right now can run without us with the right system in place. In loop, you prompt. Near loop, you respond.

This is blitzscaling for agentic engineering. It's not meditation, it's Xanax. It's not working out, it's a GLP-1. A useful local maximum for getting results at all costs. We stop worrying about getting things right and start getting things SHIPPED.

🏭 WHAT IS A TINY SOFTWARE FACTORY?
A tiny software factory is a software factory built to solve one specific problem where a proactive agent works around the clock in a durable environment with you near the loop instead of in it. One problem. One proactive agent. Around the clock. Durable. Human near the loop, not in it.

⚠️ AGENTIC ENGINEERING DONE WRONG
Tiny Software Factories is a crash course in agent anti-patterns that will NOT scale, and that's the point. The shortcuts that make a factory useful today: one agent, cron in the server, a JSON config, agent-written pages, SQLite on one box, and bash in your codebase. Each one gets you from zero to value fast. Each one breaks somewhere, and you'll know exactly where.

🚀 In this lesson, we open the empty factory: a fully built template with every feature you need and no specialization yet. Then we stack features from the feature map, ranked by value and effort:

🤖 The agent on your right: a durable agent, always on, always one message away
📋 Lists on your left: every product is a list of something. What's in your list?
🎯 Focus in the center: a generative UI where your agent builds, tweaks, and tunes pages for you
🔁 Agent access parity: everything you can do, your agent can do. Every UI control has a matching agent tool
🧠 Core four control: context, model, prompt, tools. Auto compaction, tiered model selection, a prompt engineered system prompt, every tool in view
🧩 Extensible harness: your agent is a composition of capability slices (factory, coding, pages, image generation, factory controls)
🎨 Customizable DX and UX: themes, nav bars, hotkeys, animations. Liquid software, built to be changed
⏰ Cron prompts: prompts on a schedule. Close the browser and your agent keeps working

💡 Watch the agent modify ITSELF: one prompt disables all of its coding tools and raises its own thinking level. Reflection for AI agents. Powerful, and dangerous if you don't control it.

🛠️ INITIALIZE, CONFIGURE, SPECIALIZE
With one meta skill and one command, you mount a new factory next to your codebase. Point it at your repo, drop it in a sandbox, and go from zero to a working agentic system in minutes. Every prompt, tool, hotkey, extension, and theme is accessible to you and your in-loop agent, so you build the system that builds the system.

🔥 TSF vs IA3
Tiny Software Factories is a highly compressed, lossy version of the Infinite Agentic Engineering core lessons. TSF lives near the loop: fast, rapidly deployable, intentionally imperfect. IA3 goes out the loop, where you build fully autonomous systems that operate for you without you. Know which one you're building, and why.

✅ Key takeaways:

In Loop vs Near Loop: Stop babysitting AI coding agents. Give feedback, make decisions, and approve work your agent has already done.

Data Flywheel: Every signal you give your near loop agent makes the factory better.

Proactive Agents: Durable agents plus a trigger inside a sandbox. It doesn't wait for you to work. It works for you, then waits.

Agent Cron Jobs: A name, a schedule, a prompt. The fastest path to repeat work running while you're away.

Right Model for the Job: Don't fixate on one model. Whether you route through OpenRouter or run a pi agent harness, pick the right performance, cost, speed tradeoff.

Join IndyDevDan as we build tiny software factories that work around the clock, so you can get things done at the speed of agents.

Stay focused and keep building.
IndyDevDan

AI / AI Tools / AI Agents.title: ELITE Agentic Engineers Are LEAVING THE LOOP... Here’s why
AI / AI Tools / AI Agents.description:
If your AI agent is already a better programmer inside the loop than you are on your best day, why are you still sitting in it? 🔥


🎥 VIDEO REFERENCES
• IA3 Phase 3 Presale Deal Is Live: https://agenticengineer.com/infinite-agentic-engineering?y=52JX83rGPLc
• Proactive Durable News Agent: https://youtu.be/OLqP8jxJ0Wc
• Proactive On-Call Durable Agent: https://youtu.be/DNDYYHsypZg

Mythos class models are here. Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT 6 Astra are better programmers than you are I. In fact, they're Alien Engineers. So why are you and I still sitting in the loop?

You and I are now the bottleneck. Up to 80% of the engineering work you're babysitting right now in a terminal can run without you if you have the right architecture in place. It's time to stop being the trigger for every prompt and start building the system that builds the system.

🚀 In this video, IndyDevDan breaks down the critical transition from human in the loop, to human near the loop, to finally out the loop. Phase 1 and Phase 2 of AI coding are completely saturated. Relying on out-of-the-box Claude Code or Codex sessions that die the moment you close your laptop is yesterday's advantage. The next leap in agentic engineering is building proactive agents and durable agents that start doing real work before you even sit down.

🔥 Jumping straight from in-loop prompting to full cron autonomy is hard. The bridge is moving near the loop: Prompt, Click, Cron. By combining durable agents with isolated cloud or local sandboxes and an event-driven API trigger layer, your agents stop waiting for you to work. Instead, they work for you and wait for your decision.

🛠️ We walk through three real near-loop systems running right now with the Pi coding agent, Pi Durable, and Jev:

On-Call Incident Response Agent: Streams live logs, uses Jev to classify 4xx and 5xx events in milliseconds, runs root-cause analysis, prepares the fix, and waits for a single click to deploy.

Always-On Durable News Agent: Running 24/7 on a dedicated sandbox for over a week, filtering out hype, scoring prompt injection and model benchmarks, and building a personalized signal flywheel.

Deep Jev UI Replicator: Drop in a mock design and walk away while a recursive loop builds, screenshots, and uses Jev 1.14 to hill-climb toward visual parity in a cloud sandbox.

💡 Key takeaways for moving out the loop:

Proactive vs Reactive: Stop being the sole trigger for your agents. Use webhooks, cron jobs, log streams, tickets, and Jev classifiers to kick off useful work automatically.

Durable Agents in Sandboxes: Agents need their own compute, persistent memory, multi-client access (browser, terminal, phone), and crash recovery so they aren't limited by your device.

The Core Four Multiplied: Moving out the loop requires mastering context engineering, model tokenomics, system and user prompt engineering, and custom harness engineering on top of your software engineering expertise.

Vibe Coding vs Agentic Engineering: Vibe coding is not knowing what your system does and not looking. Agentic engineering is knowing what your system does so well that you don't have to look.

🌟 Phase 3 of agentic engineering is the deprecation phase: Augment, Automate, Deprecate. The new measure of your leverage isn't how many terminals you can juggle at once, it's how many specialized agents are doing useful work for you right now while you're away from the keyboard. Next time you sit down at the terminal, ask yourself: is there a reason I'm still in the loop for this work?

Stay focused and keep building.

AI / AI Tools / AI Agents.title: My Jev Pi Durable Agent CURATES News: HYPE, FACT, or SIGNAL
AI / AI Tools / AI Agents.description:
Proactive agents don't wait for you to work. They work for you, then wait. While everyone else is stuck prompting back and forth in the loop, the best engineers are moving from in the loop, to near the loop, to completely out loop.

🚀 PUSH YOUR AGENTIC ENGINEERING TO OUT LOOP
• IA3 Phase 3 Presale Deal Is Live: https://agenticengineer.com/infinite-agentic-engineering?y=OLqP8jxJ0Wc

🎥 VIDEO REFERENCES
• Durable News Agent codebase: https://github.com/disler/pi-durable-news-agent
• Durable Pi video (previous video): https://youtu.be/DNDYYHsypZg

Most engineers are still babysitting AI in a terminal while drowning in clickbait, slop, and attention theft. Stop waiting on your agents, and stop letting your agents wait on you. 🔥

Proactive agents don't wait for you to work. They work for you, then wait. While everyone else is stuck prompting back and forth in the loop, the best engineers are moving from in the loop, to near the loop, to completely out loop.

🤖 In this video, IndyDevDan breaks down how to filter through AI hype, facts, and actionable signal using a custom Durable News Agent built on Pi Durable and the open-source pi agent harness. Instead of acting like another chat window, this system runs nonstop every single minute as a cron agent on an M4 Mac mini AI agent box and inside an exe.dev AI agent sandbox.

🔥 A proactive agent is a durable agent plus a trigger inside a sandbox. Because the agent lives behind a SQLite-backed server API, both the browser generative UI and the terminal TUI act as thin, detached clients synced in real time. My hands are off the keyboard, and the system is gathering, filtering, ranking, and curating high-signal engineering news for me without me.

🛠️ Code is now infinitely cheap and copyable. What separates elite builders today is taste, judgment, and system architecture. To protect your time and token budget, we put a fast, dirt-cheap jev classifier in front of our language models. At sub-half-second latency, jev gates irrelevant stories, deduplicates coverage, verifies claims across sources, and scores every item across three distinct buckets: hype, facts, and true actionable signal.

💡 Key takeaways:

In, Near, Out Loop: The ultimate measure of your agentic engineering skill is how many autonomous threads of work run on your behalf around the clock. Proactive agents are the missing bridge between in-loop prompting and full out loop autonomy.

Hype vs. Facts vs. Signal: Hype is unfounded excitement. Facts are objectively true (like a massive math proof dump) but not always actionable today. Signal is high-leverage information you can act on right now (like a new state-of-the-art model rollout).

The Jev Pipeline: Using a jev classifier at every stage (gather, gate, dedupe, rank) keeps tokenomics razor thin so a cron agent can sweep every minute without burning cash on expensive LLM calls.

Detached Client Architecture: Built in layers with SQLite, Pi Durable, a custom pi agent harness, and a unified SDK that powers the web generative UI, terminal TUI, CLI, and cron triggers across a local Mac mini AI agent or a cloud exe.dev AI agent sandbox.

Data Flywheel and Taste Tuning: Upvote or downvote news cards, dynamically adjust keyword and source weights in plain chat, and let two-way prompting continuously sharpen what your durable agents surface next.

🌟 Don't let AI noise steal your focus, and don't lose faith in your software engineering fundamentals. Build the system that builds the system. Clone the Durable News Agent repo, wire up your own taste profile, and start transitioning your workflow from in the loop, to near the loop, to out loop.

Stay focused and keep building.
- IndyDevDan

AI / AI Tools / AI Agents.title: Gemini 4 Carbon Is HERE! (Google's Strongest Model Yet)
AI / AI Tools / AI Agents.description:
Google DeepMind just made Gemini 4 Carbon available to everyone, only weeks after Gemini 4 Argon. In this video: who gets it and when to pick Carbon over Argon, Google's benchmark claims (#1 on CursorBench 4.0, WANDR and AutomationBench at more than 2x lower cost per task), the big jump in cybersecurity (Project Fortify, real 0-days, the Fairwind Program), the science results (40x more homologs, AlphaProof Code proving Signal's protocol), and early community tests against Claude Fable 5.2 and GPT-6.1 Sol. Then Gemini Decision 1, Google's new decision model at $0.10 per 1M input tokens, the Business Insider leak on Gemini 4 Hydrogen, the theory that OpenAI is holding GPT-6.2 Astra for Anthropic's IPO, the WSJ report on Nvidia's board and Jensen Huang, and Elon Musk's update on Grok 4.8.

For hands-on demos, tools, workflows, and dev-focused content, check out World of AI, our channel dedicated to building with these models:  ‪‪ ⁨‪‪‪‪‪‪‪@intheworldofai

AI / AI Tools / AI Agents.title: My AI Agents Write Code Faster Than I Can Verify It
AI / AI Tools / AI Agents.description:
76% of developers and engineering managers in Sonar's 2027 State of Code report say they generate AI code faster than they can verify it! And I'm right there with them, since I run software factories where agents open pull requests around the clock.

AI code looks correct way more often now, so the bugs that slip through are the subtle ones. The way I handle it in my own factories is simple. Agents can write whatever they want, but nothing merges until a check the agent doesn't control says it passes.

The full report is really worth a read if you're handing more of your code to agents: https://fandf.co/4iN1mvB

Thanks to Sonar for working with me on this!

AI / AI Tools / AI Agents.title: I Trust My AI Agents to Merge Code… But NOT Ship It
AI / AI Tools / AI Agents.description:
I trust my agents to merge code all night, but I definitely don't trust them to ship straight to production. Tests and reviews only tell you the code looks right.

LaunchDarkly helps teams control and monitor how changes behave once they're live in production. They just launched Release Autopilot, where agents do the feature flag work that used to take an engineer: risk classification, success metrics, automatic release plans that start with a canary release, feature-level observability and flag cleanup. Safe, controlled releases with guardrails.

Check out Release Autopilot: https://fandf.co/4sttJ6l

Thanks to LaunchDarkly for working with me on this! #ad

AI / AI Tools / AI Agents.title: Your Coding Agent Has a MASSIVE Blind Spot (You Need to Fix It)
AI / AI Tools / AI Agents.description:
I've had agents break hundreds of times in production (sometimes in very embarrassing ways), and almost all the time it comes down to the blind spots in my coding agent. Your agent sees your code, but not what it does once it's running.

The Dynatrace MCP Server brings live production data to the coding agent in your IDE, so you can ask about your running systems in plain language and trace a problem to the exact line behind it.

Read the walkthrough: https://fandf.co/4ik3t9P

Thanks to Dynatrace for sponsoring this video and working with me on it!

AI / AI Tools / AI Agents.title: Let's Open Source the World — Brandon Thomas, ArtCraft
AI / AI Tools / AI Agents.description:
ArtCraft’s first Photoshop approximation took about 24 hours to build, Brandon Thomas says. At CODE Summit 2026, he explains how Rust and AI coding agents power open source alternatives to Adobe’s creative tools, Microsoft Office and Figma. MCP and CLI automation, Linux support, reusable UI components and CI bottlenecks lead into Autocraft, a forthcoming software factory for issue triage, agentic development, evaluations and post training.

AI / AI Tools / AI Agents.title: "Where is all the automation?" — Diogo Almeida, TypeSafe AI
AI / AI Tools / AI Agents.description:
Being Einstein 95% of the time and Mr. Bean 5% is Diogo Almeida's analogy for unreliable LLM automation. At CODE Summit 2026, the TypeSafe AI cofounder argues that RLHF optimizes models for human assistance and makes the case for machine native AI with Jev. Reliable agents, KV cache limits, shared memory, semantic types and real time security point toward what software engineers could build beyond chatbots.

- https://x.com/CompleteSkeptic
- https://docs.typesafe.ai/introduction

AI / AI Tools / AI Agents.title: Rethinking Claude Code Best Practices — Lydia Hallie, Anthropic
AI / AI Tools / AI Agents.description:
The models have gotten really good, and most of what we've added to our Claude Code setups over the past year is now holding them back. In this talk I'll go through what Claude Code best practices look like for the Claude 5.5 models, what's still worth keeping, and what you no longer need to think about.

Speaker info:
Lydia Hallie
Member of Technical Staff, Anthropic
Lydia Hallie is a Member of Technical Staff at Anthropic, working on developer relations for Claude Code. She creates technical content, talks, and workshops that help developers understand how Claude Code works and how to use it effectively.

AI / AI Tools / AI Agents.title: Use Grok Bot Better Than 99% of People (Full Course)
AI / AI Tools / AI Agents.description:
I sit down with Ras Mic to see how he runs his work and his life through Grok Bot. He calls himself a Grok Bot maxi, and he uses it as a personal agent and as an orchestrator that hands engineering work to Claude Code. He walks me through five areas: engineering, design, content ideation, business and finance, and shopping. Along the way he shows his bots, his prompts, and the projects they shipped, including Pluto, Bezalel, a Rust trading app, and a Shopify store for his brother's clothing brand. If you ship ideas, this episode gives you a setup you can copy today.

Timestamps

00:00 – Intro
01:55 – Engineering Bot
07:57 – Why use Grok Bot as an Orchestrator
14:01 – Grok Bot + Claude Code
19:43 – Security Checks
21:54 – Designer Bot
31:12 – Content Bot
37:19 – Business & Finance Bot
42:41 – Shopping Bot
44:53 – Closing Thoughts

Key Points

• Give each serious project its own bot, keep one general engineering bot for random ideas, and delete bots once they stop being useful.
• Use Grok Bot to orchestrate and Claude Code with Opus 5.5 to write the code.
• Ras Mic says the $200-a-month Claude Code plan is worth $8,000 to $12,000 in API credits, so he leans on subscriptions.
• Lock the design in Paper before any code gets written, with a design system the agent can reference.
• A YouTube bot scans X at 9 a.m. and 5 p.m. and sends three video topics with tweets, title ideas, and resources.
• Finance bots connected through Plaid give Ras Mic's advisor bot enough context to talk him out of shiny objects.

Numbered Section Summaries

1. Engineering Bot

Grok Bot organizes work into bots, each with its own context, skills, and computer, where the ChatGPT app gives you threads that get mixed up. Ras Mic lets context decide. Pluto, his Bible app, and Bezalel (at $200 MRR) each get a bot, a general engineering bot catches random ideas like Still, a screenshot extension built in two prompts, and permanent bots handle IT and ML. When a bot stops being useful, he right-clicks and deletes it.

2. Grok Bot Orchestrates, Claude Code Builds 

Ras Mic sends ideas to his engineering bot at night and wakes up to a repo on GitHub, like the AI governance compliance app it built after a friend told him about government contracting. For Pluto, he had Grok Bot review a plan from a PDF, revise it with his feedback and a friend's, then build it with Claude Code on Opus 5.5 using /goal. The run went for hours and returned five working PRs, which people are now testing.

3. Why Grok Bot + Claude Code 

I ask why an engineer would put Grok Bot on top of Claude Code or Codex, and Ras Mic points to the UX. He works through PRs from his phone during dinner at his mom's house and talks to a bot on speaker while he drives. Grok Bot also covers the business side. While building VP Cloud, a Canadian sovereign cloud, one of his bots emailed a GPU provider on its own to ask for a discount and mentioned his YouTube subscriber count.

5. Design Bot

Ras Mic collects inspiration from X and Mobbin, sends a screenshot to his agent, and has it build a design system in Paper through the Paper MCP. He used that flow for his brother's clothing brand, where Grok Bot designed a Christian gothic storefront in Paper and then built it as a Shopify front end. 

6. Content Bot 

Twice a day, at 9 a.m. and 5 p.m., Ras Mic's YouTube bot scans X and sends three topics that fit his channel, each with source tweets, a title idea, and resources. He mostly scripts his own videos because people prefer people, and he uses an editor bot to explore styles and brief his human editor.

7. Advisor Bot

Ras Mic has shiny object syndrome, so he runs ideas past an advisor bot. His finance bots connect to his accounts through Plaid, so the advisor can read his transactions and hold him to his goals. When he sent it a real estate listing, it advised against buying, citing cash pulled from his other goals, a seller who wanted unrepresented buyers only, and a boiler and furnace from 2009.

8. Shopper Bot

Grok Bot scans eBay every day for sealed GPUs. For Ras's PS5 Pro, it emailed the seller, learned it was a store in Ontario two hours away, gave him the number to call, and bought the console once he confirmed. It also found shoes for his sciatica and emailed the list to his wife for approval.

AI / AI Tools / AI Agents.title: Claude Fable 5.2: How I’d Make Money With It
AI / AI Tools / AI Agents.description:
In this solo episode, I share 12 prompts for Fable 5.2 across four areas: making money, productivity, video and content, and hardware. I run several of them live, including an audit of my design agency, a freelance job Fable 5.2 found on Upwork, a 100-niche research sweep with subagents, and a minimalist phone it designed from one prompt. I cover why Fable 5.2 can work 10 to 12 hours on its own, why it now admits when it lacks an answer, and how to sell results as a fixed-price service. If you want to make money, get more done, or build hardware with Fable 5.2, this episode gives you prompts you can copy today.

Timestamps

00:00 – Intro
01:00 – Prompt 1: Audit Your Entire Business
02:05 – Prompt 2: A Freelance Job End to End
03:46 – Prompt 3: A Hundred Niches at Once
04:33 – Prompt 4: Rebuild the Ancient Software
05:25 – Prompt 5: Deal Checker for a Boring Business
06:54 – Results from Prompts
08:53 – Prompt 6: Grill Me
09:33 – Prompt 7: Operate Legacy Apps
10:07 – Prompt 8: Red Team My Plan
11:11 – Video and Marketing Engineering
12:39 – Prompt 9: Short-Form Editor
13:05 – Prompt 10: Niche Explainer Videos
13:24 – Prompt 11: One Episode, Every Format
13:56 – Prompt 12: One person Hardware Company
16:42 – A Minimalist Phone Idea
17:41 – Design and Mockups
18:31 – Closing Thoughts

Key Points

• Fable 5.2 works 10 to 12 hours on its own, so I hand it jobs that take a high-end consultant a week.
• Freelance jobs and software rebuilds can now sell per output, where people used to bill by the hour.
• Stronger subagents let me research 100 niches in one prompt and get back one ranked table.
• Fable 5.2 now admits uncertainty, which opens up finance and legal work like checking a seller's P&L.
• Videos at $1 to $5 each let me build faceless channels and own distribution.
• One prompt gets me a parts list, circuit design, firmware, and a printable enclosure for a device.

Numbered Section Summaries

1. Long Jobs and Freelance Work 

My audit prompt asks Fable 5.2 to review my website, pricing, onboarding, emails, and top five competitors, keep a running log, and rank the 10 changes most likely to make money, with evidence for each. For LCA, my design agency, it ranked every call with evidence and stayed to the point, as it has on every business we incubate. I asked it to find a freelance job it could do, and it picked an Upwork equity analyst report on TDMX at a $450 fixed price

2. Subagents and Old Software 

Fable 5.2 runs many subagents well, so one prompt spins up a subagent for each of 100 niches to find the top three complaints, what people pay today, and how hard each niche is to reach, then returns one ranked table and the five to build for. Another prompt hands it a spreadsheet a client has run their business on for 12 years and asks it to figure out what the sheet does, rebuild it as a simple web app

3. A Model That Admits Uncertainty 

Hallucination has held legal and finance teams back from AI, and Fable 5.2 now admits when it lacks an answer, the way a person would. My deal checker prompt hands it a seller's P&L and listing, asks it to flag everything that fails to add up, label each number verified, unverified, or suspicious, and write the 15 questions I should ask before making an offer.

4. Productivity Prompts 

The Grill Me prompt interviews me with 20 questions, one at a time, about how I make decisions in my business, then turns my answers into a skill file Fable 5.2 follows from then on. It operates a computer well, so it can open an old invoicing app, export last month's invoices, match them against the bank statement, list outstanding ones, and check with me before sending anything.

5. Video, Content, and Distribution 

My three prompts cut a raw four-minute talking-head video to its strongest 45 seconds with three hooks, build a 60-second animated niche explainer with five opening lines, and turn one transcript into a PDF playbook, five tweets in my voice, a newsletter, a two-minute free tool, and flags on any claim that needs a check.

6. Vibe Manufacturing From One Prompt 

I recall Anthropic saying in a blog post that Fable 5.2 designed three working devices from a single prompt, so my hardware prompt asks for a one-job device for one niche with a priced parts list, circuit design, firmware, a printable enclosure, and the cost to make 100.

AI / AI Tools / AI Agents.title: AI Agents are too good at marketing now
AI / AI Tools / AI Agents.description:
I sit down with Cody Schneider, to break down how to become a top 0.1% marketer with GrokBot, Claude Code, and the tools around them. Cody shows the environment an agent needs to do marketing work: data in a warehouse, write access to ad platforms, and API tools for images, video, and leads. We build static ads live for Idea Browser, Late Checkout, Cursor, and more, then make a UGC avatar video ad with motion graphics for about $5. I add two pieces of my own: a swipe warehouse of creative references and a creative director agent that scores every ad. If you build products and hear crickets, this episode gives you workflows you can set up today.

Timestamps

00:00 – Intro

Links Mentioned: 

Cody's Marketing Skills: https://startup-ideas-pod.link/cody-marketing-skills
Guide for setting up Facebook Developer Token: https://startup-ideas-pod.link/Facebook-ads-developer-token-setup

Key Points

• Agents do marketing's middle work once they have data, platform access, and tools.
• A data pipeline into a warehouse gives agents full-funnel data and keeps them off rate-limited APIs.
• Agents write to Facebook and Google Ads through their APIs and read data only from the warehouse.
• One skill turns a brand URL into five researched, on-brand static ads.
• A UGC avatar ad with motion graphics costs about $5, compared with $300 to $500 from humans.
• Creative velocity wins, since Facebook's algorithm matches good creative to the right buyer.

Numbered Section Summaries

1. Agents are now Marketers

Cody says a static ad used to need a graphic designer and a copywriter, and a UGC video needed a creator, a video editor, and a motion graphics designer. Now GrokBot, Claude Code, or Dots handles that work with code and tokens, and Mirage Tesseract one-shot edits a 90-minute podcast, cutting silence and retakes and tracking the active speaker. I see the job of anyone building a business in 2027 as building the system around these agents, and Cody compares that role to a conductor, or a StarCraft player coordinating swarms.

2. Giving Agents the Data 

Cody warns that agents querying ad APIs directly flood their context, hallucinate, or build their own local database full of duplicates. He uses Airbyte as a data pipeline from Facebook Ads, Google Analytics, HubSpot, and the payment processor into a ClickHouse data warehouse, a Graft partner. With everything in one place, the agent queries as often as it likes and ties an ad all the way to revenue and customer lifetime value.

3. Tools for Agents

The third piece is tools: Kai AI for images and video, FAL for transcription, OpenRouter for LLMs, and Git Leads or Apollo for email and person data. With these, Cody's Google Ads agent checks in real time whether each search term carries buyer intent for its landing page, auditing 5,000 terms in 20 seconds. Graft bundles the data, access, and tools, with a free start and multiplayer access for teams, and the open source route works too.

AI / AI Tools / AI Agents.title: 8 Businesses for the AI Age
AI / AI Tools / AI Agents.description:
In this solo episode, I lay out how I think about building an AI-proof business now that anyone can press a few buttons and spin up a company in seconds. Layoffs keep coming, people copy products pixel for pixel, and I still see more opportunity than ever. I walk through eight categories: atoms, permission, attention, timing, belonging, liquidity, unique data, and outcomes. I share examples like Hampton, final.com, and Cars & Bids, say how I'd rank the categories, and show how to mix them. If you're an employee looking at a startup or a founder worried about getting copied, this episode gives you a map for building something with value when AI makes software, content, and answers almost free.

Timestamps

00:00 – Intro
01:17 – Atoms: Physical Businesses
02:26 – Permission: Licenses, Regulation, and Partnerships
04:10 – Attention: Building a Media Machine
06:28 – Timing: Spotting Trends Early
08:24 – Belonging: Paid Communities and IRL Events
10:59 – Liquidity: Marketplaces
14:38 – Unique Data: Data Brokers and Curated Directories
18:31 – Outcomes: Customers Paying for Results
20:44 – Closing Thoughts

Key Points

• Physical businesses hold up against overnight clones, and I expect their valuations to rise as tech money moves in.
• Licenses, regulation, and preferred-vendor deals are permission that a copycat has a hard time getting on day one.
• Media is underrated, and AI lets you run a content machine around a micro niche.
• A first mover's product may be easy to copy, while the data, brand, and trust it collects stay AI-proof.
• Marketplaces rank among the stickiest businesses of all time, and agents let a team of one to five run one.

Section Summaries

1. Atoms and Permission 

Pixels are software businesses and atoms are physical ones, like a coffee shop or the plumber who fixes your clogged toilet. They're harder to run, they hold up against overnight clones, and I think their valuations go up once AI and tech money spots the moat. Permission covers licenses, regulation, and deals, so you could partner with a lawyer and handle marketing, growth, and AI while they run the firm.

3. Attention 

Attention is somehow underrated right now, and people follow people. I used to hate making short form video, and now Opus 5.5 is my editor, I create on my own schedule, and I got hundreds of thousands of views in the last week. I'd pick a micro niche and build a media company around it with newsletters, meme pages, or founder-led content, aiming for a trustworthy brand that people come to for that niche.

4. Timing 

I see more trends in more micro niches than ever, and sometimes I'm shocked by how few people have built for them. I'd use ideabrowser.com, GrokBot, Claude Duet, or any personal agent platform to monitor your niches, then build first, whether that's software, a physical product, or a media company. 

5. Belonging 

People are as connected as ever and feel as disconnected as ever, so I see a big opportunity in paid communities built around a shared goal, like a Circle or Skool group or a weekly virtual event that keeps people accountable. As I understand it, my friend Sam Parr's company, Hampton, runs meetups around North America for entrepreneurs doing at least $3 million a year in revenue. We threw an IRL event in Nashville last week for founders deploying agents, and demand ran past what we knew how to meet.

6. Liquidity 

People tell me software is done, and marketplaces are the example I give back. A friend of mine launched final.com, I think last week, where you bid every week on curated high-end collectible cars, and he markets it to his big Instagram audience, while Cars & Bids sold for many millions of dollars.

7. Unique Data 

You see data brokers making millions of dollars a week, and platforms like, I think, Mercor and micro1 got coding data and sold it to the big models, which stay hungry for new types of data. You can also sell access to a curated directory, and I expect a huge explosion of curated websites and apps as LLMs and social feeds give people infinite content, with polarized, gamed restaurant reviews on Google and Yelp as one example.

8. Outcomes and Mixing the Map 

Customers are starting to pay for results through automated AI services, like a creative agency that makes logos and landing pages on the fly or a machine that studies Fiverr and Upwork and bids on the work. Your defense comes from feeding the best possible agents the best data, insights, and inspiration, plus permission like a deal with a particular company.

In this Fable 5.2 video, we go through the rules for getting the most out of Claude Fable 5.2 without burning through your limit. They come from Lydia Hallie's Claude Code best practices talk, Addy Osmani's guide on which Claude model to use for each job, and Anthropic's own guide for Fable. We tested them on our own work and narrowed them down to nine.

First, a quick look at what Fable 5.2 can do. It's 20% cheaper than Fable 5.1 ($8 in and $40 out per million tokens), writes up to 30% faster and needs fewer tokens for the same work. On Anthropic's FrontierCode test, Fable 5.2 scored 49.1%, up from 32.4% for 5.1, while Opus 5.5 scored 45.5%. Those Fable 5.2 test results are strong, but per token it still costs twice as much as Opus 5.5.

Fable 5.2 vs Opus 5.5: which should you use? Anthropic says to start on Opus 5.5 and only move up when Opus on a higher effort setting can't do the job. A builder on X gave both the same one-line prompt for a 3D model. Opus 5.5 finished in 27 minutes, while Fable 5.2 took 58 and used about seven times the tokens. When we ran Opus 5.5 vs Fable 5.2 on the same feature, the work was just as good, but Fable cost about 58% more.

So if you've been reaching for Fable 5.2 on every website, animation or video editing job, start on Opus 5.5 first. Fable earns its price on big jobs, the hardest problems and 3D work. Unity said it did best at building 3D scenes from scratch, so a Fable 5.2 game or 3D scene is the right kind of job for it.

You'll also see how to run AI agents with Fable as the lead: Fable plans and checks the work, while Opus 5.5, Sonnet and Haiku do the building. Plus, how to stop the built-in Explore subagent from charging Fable prices for every file search.

Claude usage limits drain fast when Claude AI reads web pages full of junk. We tested only-cli, a free tool that cut Claude Code token use by about 21%. See where Claude limits go, how to stretch your Claude Code usage limits, and the sites where Anthropic Claude's own web tool still wins.

only-cli (oc) on GitHub: https://github.com/only-cli/oc

What we cover in this video

Where Your Claude Usage Limits Actually Go
- Why web pages eat into your Claude AI usage limits: the page code behind the text still counts as tokens
- Our Wikipedia test: one article was about 1 MB of page code and still roughly 74,000 tokens as plain text
- How Claude read it: the first 13% word for word, the next 34% summarized by Haiku, the last 53% never read
- Why that first 13% was mostly menus and language lists instead of the article
- Everything Claude reads stays in your session for every message after that, which keeps using up your Claude usage limits

What only-cli (oc) Does
- A free, open-source program to add to your AI tools. Claude Code uses it to read web pages, and it works with Codex and Cursor too
- It gives Claude a numbered outline of about 500 tokens, so Claude can pick only the part it needs
- Ready-made shortcuts for about two dozen sites, including Hacker News, GitHub and Wikipedia
- It can read pages behind your own login, using cookies you copy from your browser
- It opened npm and Stack Overflow pages in our tests after both refused Claude's own web tool

Stop Hitting Claude Code Usage Limits So Fast
- How to get better usage limits with Claude: oc doesn't raise your limit, it makes each task use less of it
- Claude only pays for the parts of a page it actually reads
- When Claude needs the whole page, oc gives it as clean text without the menus
- Where oc doesn't help: sites with an llms.txt, a plain-text copy made for models like Claude. Claude's own web tool does better there

How to Use Claude Code With oc
- Install oc with one command from its GitHub repo
- Add a line to your CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md so your agent uses oc for web content
- Install oc's skill, which teaches your agent each command and site shortcut
- Or install the plugin in Claude Code and skip the separate skill

The Same Research Task, With and Without oc
- The task: research the workflows in Anthropic's engineering blog, all 28 posts
- Both sessions split the work across five AI agents
- Without oc: about 4.9 million tokens. With oc: about 3.9 million, with the same accuracy
- With oc, the agents read every post's actual text instead of a summary of it

Claude Plans and Practical Usage
- Claude Pro usage limits and Claude Code Pro usage limits: we don't go through plan numbers here. oc works by cutting the tokens each task uses
- Claude Pro vs Max usage limits with practical usage: this isn't a plan comparison, but the research test shows practical usage in real token counts
- Claude usage limits session vs weekly: we don't compare the two, but we do show why what Claude reads stays in your session
- Claude vs ChatGPT usage limits: not compared here, but oc also works with Codex and Cursor, so it isn't only for Claude

This Claude skill, Stageshow, gives your agent the design process of Benji Taylor, head of design at X. Most skills Claude uses are just rules; this one is a full process. Learn how to use Claude skills to build animated landing page demos, and how to set up Claude Code skills and Claude AI skills.

Stageshow: https://benji.org/stageshow
Stageshow on GitHub: https://github.com/benjitaylor/skills/tree/main/stageshow

Community with All Resources: https://ailabspro.io/?v=of628n5754g

The Roundup, our daily newsletter covering the AI stories that matter. Join now: https://www.theroundup.so/

Got a software idea but don't have the team to build it? Autometa turns your ideas into production-ready software. Check out https://autometa.dev/yt to see what we can build for you.

What we cover in this video:

The problem with product demos on landing pages
- Why a plain screenshot of your app gets skipped: it's too cluttered to hook anyone
- Why asking Claude Code for an animated demo usually comes out clunky, overdone and generic
- Benji's five ways AI demos go wrong: bland, too much, wireframe, boxed and flat
- The core issue for AI agents in design: they don't have taste

What are Claude skills, and what makes Stageshow different
- What are Claude skills: written-down instructions and resources your agent reads and follows
- Stageshow is Benji's taste written down as a hundred small design decisions, so you don't have to repeat them to the agent
- It builds a stripped-down working copy of one app screen and plays a short planned story on it, with a drawn-in cursor
- It builds on the style your site already has instead of redesigning the whole page
- Claude skills vs MCP: Stageshow is a skill, not an MCP server. It's a SKILL.md file, reference files, icons and example demos, not a tool connection
- One of the new Claude skills built around a design process rather than a list of rules

Benji's seven-step design process
- Placement: still or animated, how big, and a separate phone version designed for the phone
- Look: it reads your app's colours, fonts and corner roundness
- Story: one action, three to five moments, 10 to 16 seconds
- Real example: it starts from the closest of about 40 of Benji's own demos
- Screen: only three to seven real words, the rest are text placeholder bars
- Motion: curved cursor movement, parts slide in, and a loop with no visible restart
- Self-check: it records the demo as it plays, checks every moment side by side, and since version 1.1 can't hand it over until the check passes
- Its limit, in Benji's own words: the check catches mistakes, but it can't tell you if the idea is boring
- Plus a word from our sponsor, Higgsfield

Claude skills setup
- Copy the install command from the Stageshow GitHub or website and run it in your project's terminal
- Pick your agent: by default it installs into the .agents folder that many agents already use, or you can select a specific one
- Install it for one project or every project on your computer
- A look inside: SKILL.md, app icons, reference files and a bento grid reference
- The Stageshow playground: browse every scene on phone and desktop, demos of products like Notion and Excel, and the reduced-motion version

How to use Claude skills on a real app
- Calling Stageshow with its slash command on a music beat-making app we built with Claude
- The agent records each section and checks it frame by frame
- REHEARSAL.md: the agent's handover note on which demo it started from, what it changed and what it checked
- The result: the fake animated drawing in the hero replaced by a section that matches the real app, plus animated mixer and beat arrangement pieces in the features grid
- Giving feedback in plain words, then adding the fix to the skill so the next demo doesn't repeat it

Learn Claude skills with AI Labs
- This works as a short Claude skills tutorial on one skill from start to finish: what it is, setup and use
- If you've been looking for a Claude skills course, every skill and workflow from our videos is in AI Labs Pro
- Why we rate Stageshow among the top Claude skills for anyone with an app and a landing page
- Made for people building with AI, Claude, Claude AI, Claude Code and other AI agents, on the skill format from Anthropic

AI / AI Tools / AI Agents.description:
The DeepSeek super agent fixes the biggest problem with running AI agents across multiple Claude Code sessions. We break down the DeepSeek harness, what DeepSeek tested, and how we turned it into a Claude Code workflow that built our features and fixed a bug on its own.

Thank you Mobbin for sponsoring this video! Get 20% off Mobbin Pro's annual plan for your first year at https://mobbin.com/ailabs.

Community with All Resources: https://ailabspro.io/?v=3DklR44DHnM

The Roundup, our daily newsletter covering the AI stories that matter. Join now: https://www.theroundup.so/

Got a software idea but don't have the team to build it? Autometa turns your ideas into production-ready software. Check out https://autometa.dev/yt to see what we can build for you.

This one is AI news you can actually use. DeepSeek just released a new way of working with AI agents, and it starts from a problem anyone running several Claude Code sessions has hit: a person can only keep track of about three to five sessions at once before they lose track of which one is doing what.

What the DeepSeek super agent is
- One agent you hand all your tasks to, instead of switching between sessions yourself
- DeepSeek runs theirs as an agent that's always running in the cloud, which they talk to through team chats and GitHub
- Two kinds of agents: a router that talks to you and hands out tasks, and workers that each do one task in their own context window
- The router doesn't break a task into steps the way a lead agent does with its subagents. Its only job is to keep track of the workers and hand them tasks

What DeepSeek tested
- A single session that could start subagents against their router and workers setup, five runs each
- The slowest task took 15.7 minutes with the router setup and 29.5 minutes with the single session, almost twice as long
- The single session kept doing the work itself, so every new message interrupted it, and even when told to use subagents it often didn't
- DeepSeek runs its router on a lighter model, and it answered faster as more messages came in: 6.4 seconds at about one message a minute, 1.6 seconds at about 40

How we set it up in Claude Code
- A ticket-writing skill, one of the Claude Code skills we built for this, that turns each feature into a ticket with an rd.md (what the feature needs to do) and an eval.md (how the agent checks it's done right)
- A board that shows whether each ticket is a draft, ready or done, whether it runs solo (a subagent) or team (agent teams, an experimental feature in Anthropic's Claude Code), and which ticket it's waiting on
- A router agent on Opus with high effort, told never to write anything itself, that checks every worker's results against the ticket's eval.md
- A watchdog on Sonnet that checks every 10 minutes for agents that are stuck, going in loops or waiting on each other
- Worker agents on Sonnet, so the agents the router starts don't burn through your usage limit
- A merger that combines each worker's worktree into the main branch, a checker and a tester that test the app in a real browser with Vercel's agent-browser, and a reproducer that chases down bugs

How to use Claude Code this way
- Open Claude Code as the router with the agent flag, set the permission mode to auto, and give it a ticket number
- Mark the features you want built as ready, and the router hands them out and only comes to you when there's a choice to make
- In our run, the checker found a bug that was in the app before any of the tickets, the reproducer fixed it, and the router only told us once it was fixed
- Works with any AI coding agent: run the ticket skill in whichever agent you use, and if it doesn't have agent teams, ask it to use subagents for team tickets instead

What it cost
- The router was open for about an hour and built three tickets: the team ticket ran 26 minutes before we stopped it and merged it, and two solo tickets ran at the same time in 11 and 17 minutes
- About 230,000 tokens written and about 32.7 million read, most of it agents reading parts of the conversation again, which costs way less
- More tokens than a single session, but a better app and no more juggling sessions

The full DeepSeek super agent setup from this Claude Code workflow is in AI Labs Pro.

I spent a few hours building an entire product launch from my phone using Claude Code in Claude Projects, with a mix of Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.2. AI / AI Tools / AI Agents.title: Claude Fable 5.2 is distubingly good with Blender
AI / AI Tools / AI Agents.description:
Fable 5.2 was just released and I created this video in one prompt with Blender.

I gave Claude one prompt. 

It wrote code that builds the entire room in Blender: the desk, the MacBook, the light, even Clawd.

The laptop screen is a web page Claude built to look like the Claude app, played on the laptop inside the 3D scene.

Then it animated everything itself: 13 camera shots, every single key press, Clawd jumping around, and the sun going from golden hour to night to sunrise.

It rented 10 GPUs on RunPod and rendered the whole thing in 4K in 52 minutes. Total cost: $5.75.

It graded it, added the titles, and made the music and sound effects with ElevenLabs.

The longer, deeper version of this lesson is on my Patreon: https://www.patreon.com/echohive42/posts/how-to-ask-ai-175376475

This lesson is about how those handles are found: together. I said what I did not understand about a look people loved, and asked what it was and why they loved it. I asked for five styles, each with its name, so that I could learn, and minutes later five words were enough to give a film its look: kinetic typography, plus flow fields. AI / AI Tools / AI Agents.readme_excerpt: # Claude Trading Skills **Data handling:** [Privacy policy](docs/en/privacy.md) · [Security policy](SECURITY.md) Claude Trading Skills started as a personal project to use AI to improve my own trading process. Claude Trading Skills is a Claude Skills-based trading workflow toolkit for time-constrained individual investors. It is designed for investors who use long-term investing, ETFs, and dividend stocks as their core, while using disciplined swing trading as a satellite strategy when market conditions are favorable. The goal is not to outsource buy/sell decisions to AI. The goal is to structure market review, risk management, trade planning, journaling, and continuous improvement. It is open source because the workflows, checklists, and review habits behind better trading decisions can improve through shared practice. This is not a signal service or a promise of profitability. It is a toolkit for traders who want to build a better decision process. The project follows a **first for self, open for others** stance: it is built first as a practical workflow the author uses, then shared openly for others who face similar constraints. 📖 **Documentation site:** **Project vision:** [`PROJECT_VISION.md`](PROJECT_VISION.md) 日本語版READMEは[`README.ja.md`](README.ja.md)をご覧ください。 ## Disclaimer This repository is for educational, research, and process-improvement purposes only. It is not financial advice, investment advisory service, tax advice, legal advice, a signal service, or a broker…

It flexibly transforms unconstrained pre-writing materials (ideas and experimental logs) into submission-ready LaTeX manuscripts, including comprehensive literature synthesis and generated visuals, such as plots and conceptual diagrams. Acting like an orchestrated team of specialized agents, it handles outline generation, literature review, section writing, content refinement, and plotting to close the gap between raw research materials and submission ready papers. ## Key Features - **Multi-Agent Pipeline**: Orchestrates specialized agents (Outline, Literature Review, Section Writing, Content Refinement, Plotting) for end-to-end paper generation. - **Comprehensive Literature Synthesis**: Automatically searches, prioritizes, and integrates relevant literature into the manuscript. - **Visuals Generation**: Generates plots and supports the inclusion of conceptual diagrams. - **LaTeX Automation**: Produces submission-ready LaTeX manuscripts adhering to target conference templates. ## Installation 1. **Environment Setup**: The project relies on a Conda environment named `paper_orchestra`. Earning $100,000 a year used to mean financial comfort—and just a decade ago, it put you in the upper-middle class in states like California, Washington, Colorado, and Utah. Today, that same six-figure income officially counts as lower-middle class in 15 US states.

Based on MoneyLion’s analysis using Pew Research’s middle-class definition and the latest U.S. Census data, rising median household incomes mean the goalposts have moved. In places like New Jersey, a household now needs nearly $120,000 just to exit the lower-middle-class bracket, with Delaware, Minnesota, and Rhode Island being the newest additions to the list.

Blockchain / Crypto / Web3.title: Show HN: ChainBounty – improving the blockchain funding model
Blockchain / Crypto / Web3.author: wellinever
Blockchain / Crypto / Web3.story_text: Abstract. Token-funded bounties to incentivize competition-style participation in blockchain development projects would result in wider and better allocation of investment, and allow investors to diversify exposure across a field of potentially successful projects. Overall this would increase the rate of progress within development of the blockchain space. We propose a centralised platform for the administration of token-funded bounty driven development projects whereby experts allocate pools of invested capital according to the technical merits of development projects, and investors are rewarded with token allocation in funded projects. Draft Whitepaper: http://chainbounty.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/07/chainbount... We see this as bringing a variation of the YC model to blockchain - experts select large numbers of small projects and provide them with funding to reach the next level of development. This is in contrast to heavily funded ICOs where tiny teams of developers are given hundreds of millions of dollars. After feedback from HN readers: - Do you think this model will better incentivize development in the blockchain space? - What particular challenges do you think would be useful to run? https://twitter.com/ChainBounty/ https://www.facebook.com/ChainBounty-449553402088106/

Sense-Making & Narrative Analysis.title: Learning by doing: Moore's law, Wright's law, Arrow's law
Sense-Making & Narrative Analysis.author: transhumanist_atom_understander
Sense-Making & Narrative Analysis.excerpt: Economists studying technological progress contrast invention to learning by doing. Invention is doing something new, whereas learning by doing is doing the same thing over and over. One example of invention is LED lighting. Ravers with LEDs of course look futuristic, but now that LED lighting is widespread, the whole world looks a little different, and old indoor photos look old just because of the quality of the light. It was a total trend break from the steady improvement of incandescent lighting since Edison. LED lighting required a new material: gallium nitride for the blue LED. My postdoc work was in materials discovery, and blue LEDs and lithium-ion batteries were aspirational examples. Solar power, though, was an uncomfortable reminder of how much technological progress had nothing to do with us. The solar boom was not because of academics working on exciting alternatives to silicon in the lab, but decades of accumulated progress in manufacturing with silicon. (The exception is America's only major solar cell manufacturer, First Solar; they use cadmium telluride.) I first saw a graph like this at a conference: On the y axis is log price, and on the x axis is log cumulative production: that is, how many solar panels have ever been made, measured in watts. When we see a line on a graph like this, we call it an instance of "Wright's Law". Soon enough I saw these graphs everywhere online; this one is from OWID . People call this a "learning curve" or an "experience…

Sense-Making & Narrative Analysis.title: Read More Facts and Fewer Theories
Sense-Making & Narrative Analysis.author: Arjun Panickssery
Sense-Making & Narrative Analysis.excerpt: I’m a broken record on this, but almost all of the most ~thoughtful~ people I know (or have interviewed) have memorized a lot of dates, places, names, numbers etc. And not just memorized, but care about their ability to recall specifics. Seek truth from facts. It’s the only way. — Joe Wiesenthal So many people reason through heuristics, like who is aligned with whom, what personal financial interests they might have at stake, what peer group pressure they get. And I get it, because these things are complicated. But the way out, as always, is to seek truth from facts. — Joe Wiesenthal “You open the newspaper to an article on some subject you know well. In [Murray Gell-Mann’s] case, physics. In mine, show business. You read the article and see the journalist has absolutely no understanding of either the facts or the issues. … [Then you] turn the page to national or international affairs, and read with renewed interest as if the rest of the newspaper was somehow more accurate about far-off Palestine than it was about the story you just read. You turn the page, and forget what you know.” — Michael Crichton Many who read about Diamond’s geographic determinism, Fukuyama’s end of history, Morris’s energy-capture thesis, Acemoglu and Robinson’s inclusive and extractive institutions, or Turchin’s structural-demographic theory would have been better served learning basic empirical facts about historical or present societies. There are a bunch of reasons: With basic knowledge, you can…

Sense-Making & Narrative Analysis.title: What do kill switches buy us?
Sense-Making & Narrative Analysis.author: Jacob Brinton
Sense-Making & Narrative Analysis.excerpt: Summary Installing kill switches in every US datacenter could help avert some catastrophes, and might even reduce extinction risk a little, but mainly through indirect effects. The legibility of this means it's an early choice for politicians to be seen doing something about AI risk, and could be worth advocacy energy if implementation could build into further verification/transparency efforts. That said, having kill switches in place might lower the urgency to get more robust plans to lower takeover risk and lower the chances of warning shots. Threat model There are three broad routes to AI going poorly: Loss of control Extreme power concentration Societal destabilization leading to either of the above Kill switches are a candidate to reduce the risk of #3, and might have a small role reducing the risk of #1. Takeover from reckless AIs It might be the case that the first AIs that want to accrue resources and are capable enough to do so will not have enough strategic taste to know to lay back until they are smart enough to decisively overpower humanity. In this case, having hardwired kill switches could help prevent lots of these reckless AIs from causing havoc and setting up agent civilizations on the internet. In order to avoid this, the following series of events need to happen: Monitorability can detect cases where an agent or swarm of agents is dangerous enough that we should shut down their compute. I’m not sure how quick internal monitors are, but Check Point reports…

Sense-Making & Narrative Analysis.title: Safety Cases Have an Agent Foundations Problem
Sense-Making & Narrative Analysis.author: Austin Long
Sense-Making & Narrative Analysis.excerpt: If we want to ensure that AI systems are safe, should we approach the problem like an engineer, or a scientist? Do we need to discover deep and fundamental truths about how intelligence works, or is it better to focus our efforts on applying the battle-tested methods developed by safety engineers over the course of decades? As others have noted , this question is beginning to become a crux of disagreement between those who are concerned about the risks posed by advanced AI systems, and those who are relatively confident that humanity will muddle through. In this post I argue that it isn't clear how to use these safety engineering methods, or whether they work for advanced AI systems, because you immediately run into thorny scientific problems when you try to apply them. Furthermore, these thorny scientific problems are the same ones being studied under the banner of Agent Foundations. I'll start by laying out my understanding of how safety assurance typically works. Here, I'm drawing from what I've learnt as a PhD student embedded in the University of York's safety assurance research community. Then, I'll try to apply that framework to a highly capable AI system, and discuss some problems that come up. How Does Safety Assurance Work? Safety assurance is the process of a designer convincing themselves, and other stakeholders, that their system is acceptably safe. It involves not just crafting an argument to that effect, but also gathering the evidence which supports that…
